newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Gold is at 12-year low, and still vulnerable.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gold is at 12-year low, and still vulnerable.

text.p: The gold price fell below $325 an ounce on Friday to its lowest in 12 years after news that Australia's central bank had sold bullion from its reserves.
The action fuelled investor suspicions that late 20th century nation states see their gold less as a final repository of wealth than as just another asset to be used when it is convenient to do so.

Speculators were already shy about gold and the price had been in a steady decline this year. It has now shed almost $50 since January and bullion analysts said it seemed vulnerable to further losses. South African and Australian gold shares fell with the price on Friday.
Australia's disposal of 167 tonnes of gold worth some $1.8 billion followed recent sales by central banks in Europe that had also undermined confidence in the metal.

The Australian sale "was a confirmation that central banks are really tempted to sell gold reserves," said Hanspeter Hausherr, an analyst of Swiss Bank Corporation. "Now the market is further convinced this will go on, so the prices will go still lower."
Gold prices dropped in New York trading on Thursday after the Australian news broke, going below key support at $325.10 per ounce.
Prices fell again in Asia and in early European business on Friday when gold was indicated as low as $323 before it edged up slightly.
It fixed in London on Friday morning at $325.20 an ounce, the lowest fixing since January 1986.
Some analysts said prices could steady for a while now. Business would be thin on Friday because of the U.S. Independence Day holiday. But they saw a risk of further falls ahead.
Gold's all-time high was at $850 on January 21, 1980, after the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) quadrupled the price of oil and triggered violent inflation.

But governments now mostly have bottled up the inflationary genie. New derivative financial instruments also provide alternatives to gold as investor "safe havens" against turbulence in the global economy.
So gold had been losing favour among speculators even before the alarm of recent months about what central banks were thinking.
Belgium confirmed a 203-tonne central bank sale in March 1996 and the Netherlands one of 300 tonnes in January 1997.
Worries intensified when the German government -- hitherto a pillar of rectitude in bullion -- proposed to revalue its central bank gold reserves to help meet criteria for European Monetary Union.
For its part, the Reserve Bank of Australia took the view that, although some gold was worth holding as a contingency, it no longer needed to keep 20 percent of its reserves in the metal.

One London-based analyst estimates that holding gold in reserves costs central banks worldwide $15 billion a year in lost income when compared with returns from investing in other interest-bearing assets.
Gold traders in Asia said on Friday that gold's new slide could become a rout if producers of the metal were panicked into selling.
"I think we could see a big wave of selling from producers," said Dick Gazmararian, executive vice president of Republic National Bank's Asia Pacific precious metals operations.
Raymond Chan Fat-chu, president of Hong Kong's Chinese Gold and Silver Exchange Society, said investors could follow the producers down and offload more holdings.
The gold price flop was not all bad, some analysts said.
A market shakeout below $300 per ounce may in fact be good for the market by renewing investor interest, Gazmararian said.
Chan said lower prices, if they didn't collapse completely and destroy confidence, could boost gold consumption in Asia.

"This year Hong Kong will break a record (in gold imports). When gold prices come down, gold floods here and is redistributed to neighbouring countries. It's cheap gold, and Asia is trying to beat the record again," he said.
South African gold shares fell in thin Friday trade, weighed down by bullion's overnight slide. Shortly after the start of trade the Johannesburg gold index lost three percent.
